name: Globus pallidus
func: The inner, paler part of the lentiform nucleus in the basal ganglia. It is the main output 'brake' of the basal ganglia, holding back unwanted movements and releasing the chosen ones through the thalamus.

levels.kid:
The **globus pallidus** is a small part deep in the middle of your brain. Its name means "**pale ball**," because it looks lighter than the parts around it.

Think of it like the **brakes on a bike**. Most of the time, the brakes are on, so your body does not wiggle and jerk around.

When you decide to move, like waving hello, other parts of your brain tell the globus pallidus to let go of the brakes just for that movement. Then your hand can wave!

If the brakes are too tight, moving gets slow and stiff. If they are too loose, the body makes extra moves it did not mean to make.
levels.hs:
The **globus pallidus** is the inner part of the **lentiform nucleus**, lying just **medial** to the **putamen**, separated from it by the **lateral medullary lamina**. On its inner side is the **internal capsule**, which separates it from the **thalamus** behind and the caudate head in front. Below it lie the substantia innominata, the optic tract and the amygdala region. It looks pale because many myelinated nerve fibers run through it.

A thin sheet called the **medial medullary lamina** divides it into two parts:

- **Globus pallidus externus (GPe)**, the outer segment, next to the putamen.
- **Globus pallidus internus (GPi)**, the inner segment, closer to the internal capsule.

**What it does:** the GPi is one of the main **output stations** of the basal ganglia. Its neurons are always firing and release **GABA**, an inhibitory chemical, onto the **thalamus**, keeping it held back like a brake. When the striatum (putamen and caudate) chooses a movement, it briefly silences specific GPi neurons. This releases the thalamus, which then excites the motor cortex, and the chosen movement happens. The GPe helps regulate this system as part of the **indirect pathway**.

The globus pallidus also has a smaller **ventral pallidum**, below the anterior commissure, which is linked to motivation and reward.
levels.college:
Its developmental origin has been debated: older texts describe it as **diencephalic**, while modern work traces most pallidal neurons to the **medial ganglionic eminence** of the telencephalon. In rodents, GPi is called the **entopeduncular nucleus**.

**Connections:**
- **Inputs:** GABAergic **striatal MSNs** (direct pathway to GPi; indirect pathway to GPe), glutamatergic **subthalamic nucleus (STN)**, and dopamine from the substantia nigra.
- **GPe → STN** (GABA) and back, forming a reciprocally connected loop; GPe also projects to GPi, SNr and back to the striatum.
- **GPi outputs** (GABA) leave through two bundles:
  - The **ansa lenticularis**, looping around the internal capsule from below.
  - The **lenticular fasciculus (field H2 of Forel)**, passing through the internal capsule.
  These merge in **field H of Forel** and join the **thalamic fasciculus (H1)** to reach the **VA and VL** thalamus, plus fibers to the **centromedian nucleus**, lateral habenula and **pedunculopontine nucleus** in the brainstem.

GPi and the **substantia nigra pars reticulata (SNr)** together form the output nuclei of the basal ganglia; SNr mainly controls eye movements (via the superior colliculus) and head and neck movements.

**Blood supply:**
- The **anterior choroidal artery** (from the internal carotid) supplies most of GPi.
- The **lateral lenticulostriate arteries** (from the MCA) supply GPe.
- Some supply from the medial lenticulostriate arteries and posterior communicating artery branches.

**Imaging:** on T2 MRI, the globus pallidus is normally darker than the putamen in adults due to **iron deposition**, which increases with age. Its pale appearance on fresh brain slices reflects heavy myelination.
levels.phd:
**Firing:** GPi and GPe neurons fire spontaneously at high rates (often around 50–100 Hz in primates), providing constant **tonic inhibition** of their targets. Movement is permitted by a **pause** in GPi firing (disinhibition), a principle shown in the oculomotor system, where SNr neurons pause just before a saccade, releasing the superior colliculus (Hikosaka and Wurtz).

**Center-surround model:** Mink proposed that the direct pathway produces a focused pause in GPi neurons controlling the selected movement, while the subthalamic nucleus excites a broad surround of GPi neurons to suppress competing movements.

**GPe is more than a relay:** GPe contains at least two main neuron types: **prototypic neurons** (parvalbumin-positive, projecting to STN) and **arkypallidal neurons** (projecting back to the striatum). Arkypallidal neurons fire when actions are canceled, sending a broad "stop" signal to the striatum (Mallet 2016). The GPe-STN loop can generate **oscillations**, and in Parkinson disease it becomes synchronized at **beta frequencies**.

**Rate vs pattern models:** the classic Albin-DeLong model explains hypokinetic and hyperkinetic disorders by GPi firing rate: too much output (Parkinson) or too little output (chorea, ballism). But lesioning GPi improves *both* Parkinson symptoms and levodopa-induced dyskinesias, which the rate model cannot explain. This suggests that **abnormal patterns** of firing (bursting, synchrony and oscillations) matter more than rate alone, and that removing a "noisy" output may be better than transmitting it.

**Reward:** the GPi border region projecting to the **lateral habenula** carries negative reward signals and may help drive dopamine dips after disappointing outcomes (Hong and Hikosaka).

**Ventral pallidum** neurons encode the pleasantness of tastes; hotspots there amplify "liking" responses in rodents (Berridge).
levels.expert:
**Deep brain stimulation (DBS) of GPi** is a main surgical therapy for:
- **Parkinson disease:** improves "off" period slowness, rigidity and tremor, and strongly reduces **dyskinesias**. GPi and STN targets give similar motor benefit overall; teams choose based on symptoms and cognitive and mood factors.
- **Dystonia:** sustained muscle contractions causing twisting postures. GPi DBS is especially effective in **DYT1 (TOR1A) generalized dystonia**, with gradual improvement over weeks to months.
- **Tourette syndrome** in selected severe cases (GPi or centromedian thalamus).

Targeting uses MRI (often with direct visualization) and **microelectrode recording**: the GPe has slower firing with pauses, then a quiet border cell zone, then GPi with fast regular firing. Just below the target lies the **optic tract**; stimulating it causes flashes of light, a useful landmark. Medial is the **internal capsule**, which causes muscle contractions if stimulated.

**Pallidotomy:** a lesion in the posteroventral GPi, done with radiofrequency, radiosurgery or **focused ultrasound**, is an older alternative, mostly used on one side because two-sided lesions risk speech and swallowing problems.

**Disease and imaging:**
- **Kernicterus:** in newborns with very high bilirubin, the globus pallidus shows T1 and later T2 signal changes, causing a movement disorder called choreoathetosis.
- **Hypoxic injury** can damage the pallidum.
- **PKAN** (pantothenate kinase-associated neurodegeneration, a type of NBIA) shows the "**eye of the tiger**" sign: dark iron-laden pallidum with a central bright spot on T2.
- **Chronic liver disease** causes symmetric **T1 hyperintensity** of the pallidum (from manganese buildup); it can improve after transplant.
- **Progressive supranuclear palsy** involves pallidal degeneration.

Lesions of the GPi can cause dystonia or apathy; **hemiballism** (wild flinging movements) classically comes from the nearby subthalamic nucleus instead.

keyPoints: Inner, paler part of the lentiform nucleus, medial to the putamen
GPi = main inhibitory (GABA) output to the thalamus: the brake
Output via the ansa lenticularis and lenticular fasciculus
GPi supplied mainly by the anterior choroidal artery
GPi DBS treats Parkinson disease dyskinesias and dystonia

test.q: The globus pallidus lies on which side of the putamen?
test.explain: It forms the inner part of the lentiform nucleus.

test.q: Which neurotransmitter do GPi output neurons release?
test.explain: Their constant GABA release inhibits the thalamus.

test.q: Which artery supplies most of the GPi?
test.explain: The anterior choroidal artery from the internal carotid supplies GPi.

test.q: During GPi DBS surgery, stimulating just below the target causes flashes of light because of the nearby:
test.explain: The optic tract runs just under the posteroventral GPi.

test.q: The 'eye of the tiger' MRI sign appears in the globus pallidus in which condition? (abbreviation)
test.explain: Iron makes the pallidum dark with a bright center on T2.

test.q: Movement is allowed when GPi neurons:
test.explain: A pause in GPi firing disinhibits the thalamus.
